⚡ Reliability / Operations

NERC
↓
sets standards
WECC
↓
audits & enforces
RC (WECC RC)
↓
wide-area oversight
CAISO (ISO / BA)
↓
real-time dispatch
TO / TOP
↓
transmission limits
GOP (you)
Mandatory. Non-compliance = NERC violation. RC can override everyone except emergency safety.

💰 Commercial / Merchant

PSE / Merchant Owner
↓
owns the revenue
PPA (contract limit)
↓
defines max MW & price
SC (market bid)
↓
submits bids to CAISO
GOP (you)
Contractual. Violating PPA is financial, not a grid violation — but still matters commercially.

⚠ When the two chains conflict

CAISO dispatches you to 80 MW. Your PPA cap is 75 MW. Follow CAISO. Log the exceedance, notify SC/PSE, document it.

RC issues an emergency directive to reduce output immediately. RC overrides everything — execute first, document simultaneously, notify SC after.

The DP limits interconnection because of distribution voltage issues. That's a reliability constraint — follow it like a TOP curtailment.

When instructions stack up and conflict, this is the order you follow. No exceptions.
1
Emergency / Safety

Immediate threat to life, equipment, or grid stability. Your SOPs and judgment. Nothing overrides this.

2
RC Emergency Directive

The RC has wider-area visibility. Their emergency instruction can override the ISO. Rare — but when it comes, it takes the chain.

3
CAISO real-time dispatch

A DOP or direct CAISO instruction is a reliability obligation. Log it, execute it, document deviations with justification.

4
Transmission constraint (TOP / DP)

TOP curtailment orders, DP interconnection limits — both are reliability constraints overriding your dispatch target.

5
Plant physical limits

Ramp rates, inverter limits, transformer ratings. Never dispatch to a point that damages equipment.

6
PPA / Commercial limits

Last in the reliability stack. Exceeding or missing it due to grid instructions is force-majeure, not a violation on your part.

"Grid first, plant second, contract third. Log everything, call everybody, explain later."
RC Directive

RC issues wide-area emergency curtailment

▾
Setup: Grid event in the Western Interconnection. WECC RC calls CAISO and issues an emergency directive to curtail specific resources including yours. CAISO may not yet have updated your DOP.
1
RC directive received (via CAISO or directly). This is a wide-area stability instruction — highest reliability authority below emergency safety.
2
Execute immediately. Read back per COM-002. Do not wait for your DOP to update — RC instructions act on the grid faster than market signals.
3
Notify SC and log. Timestamp the directive receipt, who issued it, the MW instruction, and your confirmation. This is your paper trail.
4
Monitor for CAISO DOP update. CAISO will catch up — but you executed on RC authority. The two should align quickly.
Operator action: RC authority > CAISO DOP. Execute, read back, notify SC, log everything.
DP Constraint

Distribution Provider limits your interconnection output

▾
Setup: Your plant interconnects at distribution voltage. The DP calls with a curtailment — local distribution feeder is overloaded and voltage is out of band. Your CAISO DOP is 50 MW but the DP says hold to 30 MW.
1
DP curtailment received. This is a distribution-level reliability constraint. Treat it like a TOP curtailment — it's a physical limit on what the grid can safely absorb at your POI.
2
Confirm and read back. "Confirmed, holding to 30 MW, feeder voltage constraint." Log time and who issued.
3
Execute curtailment. You are now deviating from your CAISO DOP — this needs to be documented.
4
Notify CAISO of deviation. Log the DOP vs actual discrepancy and the reason (DP constraint, feeder name/ID). CAISO state estimator needs to know.
5
Notify SC/PSE. Lost 20 MW — commercial position is affected. SC needs to adjust their market exposure.
Operator action: DP limit is a reliability constraint. Follow it, notify CAISO, then notify SC.
PPA Conflict

CAISO dispatches below PPA minimum

▾
Setup: PPA requires 60 MW minimum. CAISO sends a 40 MW DOP due to local congestion.
1
CAISO sends DOP: 40 MW. This lands in your EMS as a new dispatch target.
2
Execute. Ramp to 40 MW per your unit's ramp rate. Do not hold at 60 MW "for the PPA."
3
Notify SC/PSE immediately. Call or log that a CAISO curtailment is active and you are below PPA minimum. Give them MW and timestamp.
4
Document everything. DOP receipt time, ramp, PPA deviation, notification. This is your force-majeure paper trail.
Operator action: Follow CAISO, notify SC, document. The commercial fix is not your problem to solve in real time.

Comparison tool — exploring proposed shift structures, not yet finalized
⚠ Draft / under review — these are candidate schedules for evaluating a potential shift structure change. Nothing here is in effect. The current live rotation is unaffected.

How the schedule works

  • Two fixed halves — Front Half (Sun–Tue + alternating Wed) · Back Half (alternating Wed + Thu–Sat)
  • 12-hour shifts — Days 6am–6pm · Nights 6pm–6am
  • Weekly rotation — D1 → D2 → D3 → N1 → N2, repeating every 5 weeks
  • Wednesday alternates between halves each week
  • Result — Fixed days on/off · only your role changes week to week

Team setup

  • Use the → BH / ← FH button to move operators between halves
  • Position = starting role — slot 1 = D1, slot 5 = N2
  • Use the ▲ ▼ arrows to reorder within a half
  • Use ✕ to remove an operator — the rotation adjusts automatically
  • Switch to Individual, Crew, or Calendar view to explore the schedule
📅
Your days never change
Front half always owns Sun–Tue. Back half always owns Thu–Sat. Plan your life a year out without guessing.
⚖
Fair rotation, no favorites
Every operator cycles through every role — D1, D2, D3, nights — on the exact same schedule. Nobody is stuck on nights permanently.
🤝
Consistent teammates
You work alongside the same half every shift. You know your crew, they know you — better communication, fewer handoff errors.
💵
Your paycheck stays the same
Same total hours as the existing schedule means your base pay and overtime don’t change. No surprises on payday — what you earn now is what you’ll earn on this schedule.

How the schedule works

  • 10 operators, 5 daily roles — D1, D2, D3 cover day shifts · N1, N2 cover nights — all five filled every day
  • 12-hour shifts — Days 6am–6pm · Nights 6pm–6am
  • Real rotation, not a formula — each operator's actual pattern, pulled directly from your live schedule. Some cycle through all five roles; others work a consistent subset
  • Verified — matches your source schedule day-for-day across the full mapped year
  • Result — Familiar patterns · complete daily coverage · a full year already mapped out

Using this view

  • Pick an operator in Individual view to see their complete year-long schedule with role by day
  • Use Crew by Day to see exactly who’s covering each role on any specific date
  • Use Calendar to see monthly coverage — highlight any operator to track their working days
  • Use this as your baseline when comparing against the Split or Pitman proposals
📋
The schedule you already know
No learning curve. No adjustment period. These are the patterns your team already runs. Use this view to see your current schedule clearly before deciding on any change.
📅
A full year of visibility
Every operator’s schedule is mapped through June 2027. Plan PTO, medical appointments, and life around a schedule you can actually see — 12 months out.
✅
Five roles covered daily
D1 through N2 is staffed every single day of the year. No coverage gaps, no role going unfilled, no scrambling last minute when someone calls out.
🔍
Your comparison baseline
Toggle between this and the Split or Pitman proposals to see exactly how your personal days and roles would shift. Make an informed call with real schedule data.

How the schedule works

  • Two squads alternate — Squad A and Squad B never work the same day, ever
  • 2-2-3 pattern — Work 2 days, off 2, work 3 days, off 2, work 2, off 3 — then repeat
  • 12-hour shifts — Days 6am–6pm · Nights 6pm–6am
  • Roles rotate each cycle — D1 → D2 → D3 → N1 → N2 across the full rotation
  • Result — Longer stretches off · predictable long weekends · same crew every shift

Using this view

  • Pick an operator in Individual view to see every day they work and their role for that day
  • Use Crew by Day to see the full 5-person crew for any specific date
  • Use Calendar to see a full month at a glance — highlight any operator to track their pattern
  • Squad A chips are blue · Squad B chips are green
🔄
More consecutive days off
The 2-2-3 pattern gives you 2 or 3 days off at a stretch, consistently. That’s enough time to actually decompress — not just recover before the next shift.
⚖
Fair rotation built in
Every operator cycles through D1, D2, D3, N1, and N2 across the full schedule. The pattern does the work — no manager has to police who gets the good shifts.
📅
Plan your life a year out
The 2-2-3 cycle repeats like clockwork. Once you know your squad and start date, you can map out every off day for the next year without asking anyone.
🤝
Tight crew, every time
You work every single shift alongside the same 4 teammates. That consistency builds the kind of trust that makes shift handoffs fast and incidents rare.
